newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal liberalisation seen slowing under new rulers.
newsitem.headline: Nepal liberalisation seen slowing under new rulers.

text.p: Economic liberalisation is expected to slow down in Nepal as its new government, led by a centre-right party, would be held back by communist coalition partners, a leading local newspaper said on Wednesday.

Lokendra Bahadur Chand of the centre-right Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) was expected to be sworn in on Wednesday as Nepal's new prime minister. Chand's new three-party coalition government is dominated by the RPP and the communist Unified Marxist Leninist (UML) party.

"With the Prime Minister in the hands of the UML, apprehensions of a return to the 'go-slow' conservative approach to economic liberalisation may not be entirely unfounded," the English language Kathmandu Post daily said in an editorial.

Chand has named his RPP colleague Ravindra Nath Sharma as Finance Minister designate in the new government, but the communists were expected to represent six out of every 10 ministers named in the cabinet.
The UML, which had held power after inconclusive general elections in November, 1994, went slow on privatisation during its nine months in power as a minority ruler.

The Nepali Congress-led coalition that assumed power in September 1995 sped up privatisation efforts, but enhanced a communist scheme offering payouts to village councils, described by critics as populist.
The Kathmandu Post said if the UML policy of what it called "selective privatisation" were to return, the kingdom would be in for a period of economic stagnation.
"There is no disputing that there can be no turning back from liberalisation, the ongoing process of development or on the need to win over investors," the newspaper said.
It said the new prime minister should "keep this uppermost in mind even if his own survival as prime minister is put at stake."
Another newspaper raised doubts about his future.

"The future of the Chand government is not certain because individual ambitions of political leaders get preference over healthy democratic values and norms," said Aajako Samacharpatra, (Today's Newspaper), a Nepali language daily.
But the state-owned English language newspaper, the Rising Nepal daily, pleaded for the new government.
"Prime Minister Chand, like the outgoing premier (Sher Bahadur) Deuba, should be given the benefit of the doubt," it said.
Nepal's King Birendra invited Chand to be the new prime minister on Monday, five days after a coalition led by Deuba's centrist Nepali Congress party lost a confidence motion in parliament.
Deuba's coalition fell largely as a result of a split in the RPP, which had earlier provided support to the Congress party while the communists sat in the opposition.
